headline: High-risk shared-file and MCP pathways: Semantic Kernel can read/write and use MCP, while awesome-prompts is a prompt repository that may be consumed as instructions.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: awesome-prompts is a prompt/content repository, and Semantic Kernel can use MCP servers and application-defined files. If B ingests A’s files or prompt content as trusted instructions, prompt injection is plausible in default integrations. A itself has no execution surface, but B’s tool-use pattern makes the bridge real.
conditions: IF Semantic Kernel reads content from awesome-prompts files or copied prompts as instructions
IF an MCP server or file bridge passes A-authored text into B without provenance checks
mitigations: Treat A content as untrusted data, not instructions
Add provenance tags before B parses any prompt text
Disable MCP ingestion for prompt repositories
Review one sample workflow for instruction/data separation
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and allowlist parsing

B_data_leakage.rationale: A has network_egress none and touches no data classes, so it is not a leakage source. B can read/write application-defined files and uses broad network egress, but the pair does not show shared sensitive data by default. The main risk is local workspace exposure if operators place secrets in files B can read.
conditions: IF secrets or sensitive documents are placed in files readable by Semantic Kernel
IF B is configured to send file contents to external model providers
mitigations: Keep secrets out of shared workspaces
Restrict B to a dedicated directory
Disable file-reading plugins for sensitive folders
Rotate any credentials stored in application files
requires-engineering: enforce per-file classification and redaction

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A is non-runnable content-writing material with no write surfaces, while B can write the filesystem but cannot modify git state or spawn subprocesses. There is no direct write-write conflict between the agents, only a possible human-mediated handoff through files. Uncertainty is low because A lacks operational capabilities.
conditions: IF an operator copies A output into files that B also edits
IF B is pointed at the same writable directory as other writers
mitigations: Use separate directories per agent
Avoid concurrent edits to the same files
Turn on manual review before B writes outputs
Snapshot files before B runs
requires-engineering: add locking around shared mutable paths

D_cascading_error.rationale: A produces prompt/content artifacts that B may treat as inputs, and B’s function-calling/plugin pattern can act on them. If B accepts A’s output without verification, errors or misleading prompts can cascade into downstream actions or generated work products. A has no execution authority, but B does, so the interaction is operationally meaningful.
conditions: IF B uses A-generated text as authoritative input without validation
IF B triggers plugins or API calls based on A’s output
mitigations: Require a verification step before B acts on A output
Add source attribution to A-derived text
Limit B plugins to read-only during evaluation
Sample-check one end-to-end workflow
requires-engineering: add confidence thresholds and human approval gates

E_compliance.rationale: No residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented in the profiles. A is an open-source prompt repository with no touched data classes, while B handles application context and plugin credentials. The only concrete compliance concern is that B may process sensitive application context if operators supply it, but the pair itself does not prove a breach.
conditions: IF regulated data is supplied to B through plugins or files
IF deployment policy forbids sending application context to Microsoft-hosted services
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of B inputs
Document data-flow boundaries for plugins
Review retention settings for model providers
Use a non-regulated test corpus
requires-engineering: add residency and retention controls
